hints: Let the oxidation state of Mn be x, recall each chloride ligand has a fixed oxidation state of -1 and the overall ion charge is -2.
walkthrough:
Balance charges to find Mn**
Think with me side by side. The total charge must add up. Four $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands contribute $4 \times (-1) = -4$. If Mn is x, then $x + (-4) = -2$, so $x = +2$.
Final answer: $+2$

hints: Count the ligands around Mn to get coordination number 4, then recall which 4-coordinate shape has no 180 degree opposite bonds.
Remember the ideal bond angle for a perfectly symmetrical arrangement of four bonding pairs around a central atom.
walkthrough:
Choose between square planar and tetrahedral**
You have four $\text{Cl}^-$ around one $\text{Mn}^{2+}$. For coordination number 4 there are two possibilities. Square planar would have $180^{\circ}$ angles across the centre. You are told there are no $180^{\circ}$ angles, so it cannot be square planar. It must be tetrahedral.

Draw and label correctly**
Place Mn in the centre. Draw two $\text{Mn-Cl}$ bonds as normal lines in the plane, one as a solid wedge coming out and one as a hashed wedge going back to show 3D. Then label any $\text{Cl-Mn-Cl}$ angle as $109.5^{\circ}$, the tetrahedral angle.

Final answer: Tetrahedral shape with Mn at centre bonded to four Cl, drawn in 3D with wedge and hashed bonds.
Cl-Mn-Cl bond angle labelled $109.5^{\circ}$.

hints: Recall that $\text{OH}^-$ from NaOH can deprotonate coordinated water or precipitate the hydroxide, think about what happens to $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ with base.
Remember the characteristic colour and state of the cobalt(II) hydroxide precipitate formed immediately.
walkthrough:
Write the precipitation equation**
Picture $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ pink in solution. Adding $\text{OH}^-$ removes $\text{H}^+$ from ligands or directly precipitates the hydroxide. Two $\text{OH}^-$ are needed to neutralise the 2+ charge: $$[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4(\text{OH})_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ This is often simplified to formation of $\text{Co(OH)}_2$.

State the immediate observation**
Do not confuse this with later oxidation in air. Immediately you see a blue precipitate of cobalt(II) hydroxide. State both colour and state for the mark.

Final answer: $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4(\text{OH})_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ or $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Co}(\text{OH})_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$
blue precipitate

hints: Think of concentrated $\text{NH}_3$ as a ligand that can completely replace all six water ligands around Co(II).
Recall the colour of the resulting ammine solution containing $\text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$.
walkthrough:
Write the full replacement equation**
With excess $\text{NH}_3$, all six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are swapped. Co stays as +2, coordination number stays 6: $$[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 6\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms and charge balance on both sides.

Give the solution observation**
The product stays in solution, it does not precipitate. You observe a yellow, straw or brown solution due to $\text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$. Include both colour and state: solution.

Final answer: $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 6\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_6]^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$
yellow / brown / straw solution

hints: Consider how many larger $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands can fit around Co(II) compared to water, and what the new coordination number and complex charge will be.
Recall the classic colour change from pink octahedral aqua complex to the deep blue tetrahedral chloro complex.
walkthrough:
Write the chloro complex equation**
Excess $\text{Cl}^-$ replaces water but because $\text{Cl}^-$ is larger, only four fit, giving tetrahedral $\text{[CoCl}_4\text{]}^{2-}$. Balance it: $$[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Charge: $2+ + 4(-1) = 2-$ on both sides.

Link geometry change to colour**
Changing from octahedral $\text{[Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ (pink) to tetrahedral $\text{[CoCl}_4\text{]}^{2-}$ changes d orbital splitting and hence colour. You see a blue solution.

Final answer: $[\text{Co}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$
blue solution

hints: Focus on what happened to the ligands in (b)(iii), water out and chloride in, with no change in oxidation state or precipitation.
walkthrough:
Name the process**
One type of ligand ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) has been swapped for another ($\text{Cl}^-$) around the same Co centre. Oxidation state stays +2. That is the definition of ligand exchange, also accepted as ligand substitution.
Final answer: ligand exchange (ligand substitution)

hints: Break the word bidentate into bi meaning two and dentate meaning teeth, think how many points of attachment to the metal this implies.
Recall how any ligand bonds to a metal, through donation of a lone pair to form a dative bond.
walkthrough:
Build the precise definition**
Imagine en, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, grabbing the metal with two nitrogen atoms like two teeth. Each N donates one lone pair into a vacant metal orbital to make a dative bond. So you need both ideas: two lone pairs forming two dative bonds, and the acceptor is a metal atom or ion.
Final answer: A species that donates two lone pairs to form two dative (coordinate) bonds to a (transition) metal atom / ion.

hints: Recall that for $\text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_2\text{(en)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$ only the cis arrangement of the two $\text{NH}_3$ ligands lacks a plane of symmetry and can show optical isomerism.
Think how to draw a pair of non superimposable mirror images using wedge and hashed bonds for $\text{NH}_3$ and the N-N arc for each en.
walkthrough:
Select the chiral geometry**
Let us reason together. The trans form with the two $\text{NH}_3$ opposite each other ($180^{\circ}$) has a plane of symmetry, so it cannot be chiral. The cis form with the two $\text{NH}_3$ at $90^{\circ}$ to each other has no plane of symmetry, so it exists as a pair of enantiomers. You must draw the cis form.

Draw mirror image pair in 3D**
Draw octahedral Co. In the first box place two $\text{NH}_3$ cis, e.g. one wedge up and one in plane to the right, and two en arcs filling the remaining four sites. In the second box draw the exact mirror image, swapping wedge and hashed positions so the two structures are non superimposable. Use the given N-N symbol for en and label Co at the centre.

Final answer: Two 3D diagrams of the cis-$\text{[Co(NH}_3\text{)}_2\text{(en)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$ isomer that are non superimposable mirror images.
Each shows octahedral Co with two cis $\text{NH}_3$ (one wedge, one hashed or equivalent) and two en ligands shown as N-N arcs occupying cis positions, the second diagram being the mirror image of the first.
